strengths: The paper studies a practically relevant question: whether an optimizer that improves predictive accuracy can increase membership privacy risk.

The empirical observation recurs across five datasets and additional architectures. On CIFAR-100, SAM improves test accuracy from 80.30% to 81.60% while modified-entropy attack accuracy increases from 77.30% to 79.25%.

The memorization and influence analyses move beyond aggregate accuracy and suggest a plausible connection to learning rare, useful patterns. The qualitative examples and synthetic construction help communicate this hypothesis.
weaknesses: The theoretical results have substantial proof gaps. In Appendix C, Lemma 3 infers vanishing test-noise contributions from near-orthogonality without establishing the necessary coefficient or norm bounds; the conditional variance is ||w3||². Theorem 2 also treats noise false-positive rates as unchanged across models, although they depend on ||w||, which the MSA ordering does not fix. Assumption 4 controls only minority coefficients. Neither theorem establishes that SAM produces the required ordering relative to SGD.

The central accuracy decomposition compares different populations. Appendix F.2 constructs separate buckets for SAM and SGD; their approximately 1,900 bucket-1 examples share only 1,116 indices. Consequently, Figure 4 cannot establish that SAM improves accuracy on the same atypical examples. Both models should be evaluated on a common, fixed partition.

The proposed entropy metric is not well-defined as written. Influence scores can be negative, and normalization is undefined when all scores are zero. Appendix F.2 nevertheless assigns all-zero cases to the highest-entropy bucket. Zero influence does not establish broadly distributed positive support, and selecting the most influential training examples within this bucket produces arbitrary ties.

The claimed mechanism remains suggestive rather than demonstrated. Memorization-score ranges are interpreted as rare subclass patterns versus noise without systematic validation. Selecting the top 20 influential examples per interval cannot establish population-wide behavior. There is no direct analysis connecting increased memorization to increased attack success on the corresponding samples, and the synthetic experiment does not evaluate privacy.

The privacy evaluation lacks strong calibrated attacks such as LiRA and reporting of TPR at low false-positive rates. The five repetitions vary attack-data splits, leaving variability across independently trained target models unquantified; several tabular improvements are small. The Sharp comparison also substantially reduces predictive accuracy, so it does not isolate flatness as the cause of reduced leakage.

The framing overstates a contradiction with generalization theory. Lower test error alone does not demonstrate a smaller train–test loss gap, and improved generalization does not guarantee lower membership risk. Training losses and generalization gaps are not reported. The SAM-specific contribution should also be distinguished more carefully from the established relationship between beneficial memorization and long-tailed data.

Reproducibility of the central influence analysis is insufficient. SAM scores are compared with externally released SGD scores without clearly documenting matched architectures, training configurations, estimation budgets, and uncertainty. The manuscript also lacks a clear manuscript-specific link to the promised score release.
